newsitem.title: UK: KPMG says worries over UK budget dampen new issues.
newsitem.headline: KPMG says worries over UK budget dampen new issues.

text.p: Fears of changes to the UK Advanced Corporation Tax (ACT) structure after the UK budget on July 2 are undermining a fragile market in new share issues, accountancy company KPMG said on Monday.

KPMG said institutional investors were concerned that the 20 percent tax credit on companies' dividend payments could be reduced or abolished following the budget, reducing their enthusiasm for new share issues.

Neil Austin, head of new issues at KPMG Corporate Finance, said the subsequent fall in dividend income from holding equities, should the tax credit be reduced, could force institutions to switch more funds into fixed income investments, such as UK gilts.
"The best we can hope for is that the Chancellor's announcement clarifies the tax position fully, so that the market can properly digest its impact and then start looking ahead again," said Austin.
According to a survey by KPMG, the level of new issue activity has dropped in 1997 compared with the previous year.
KPMG said in the first six months of 1997 2.77 billion was raised from flotations -- including Norwich Union -- compared with 4.99 billion for the first half of 1996.
Austin attributed part of the fall in new issue activity to institutions becoming more selective in their support for flotations.
"Fund managers have seen so many new issues recently, they are now looking harder for companies with real potential which are reasonably priced," Austin said.

As if to illustrate recent investor caution over the new issue market, both Ethical Holdings and Akhter Group Plc last week separately postponed plans for flotations on the London Stock Exchange, citing the forthcoming budget and negative sentiment towards smaller and mid-cap stocks as the reasons.
However, KPMG said the current nervousness was a temporary setback caused by the impending budget and the forthcoming quieter summer months.
The accountancy company believed shares in smaller companies could soon begin to catch up with shares in larger companies.

Austin argued that the recent underperformance by the FT SmallCap index against the FTSE 100 index could be explained as an exceptionally strong rise by the latter, which has been pushed higher by bid speculation and new issue activity in the financials sector.
The FTSE SmallCap index has underperformed the FTSE 100 by around 10 percent since the beginning of the year and over 20 percent in the last 12 months.
